definition: One of the chief administrative divisions or provinces of the Ottoman Empire.
etymology: From Ottoman Turkish ولایت (vilayet, “province”), from Arabic وِلَايَة (wilāya, “province, administration”). Doublet of wilaya, wilayat, and Blighty.

definition: A poem written in tercets with but two rhymes, the first and third verse of the first stanza alternating as the third verse in each successive stanza and forming a couplet at the close.
etymology: From the French villanelle, from Italian villanella, from villano (“peasant”), from Latin vīllānus (“farmhand”), from vīlla (“estate”). The origin references the pastoral themes originally associated with this form.

definition: Abounding in, or covered with, fine hairs, or a woolly substance; shaggy with soft hairs; nappy.
A bond of union; a tie.
etymology: From Latin vinculum (“bond, link”), from vinciō (“bind, fetter, tie”) + -ulum.

definition: Resembling violets in color; bluish purple.
An arrow, having a rotary motion, formerly used with the crossbow.
etymology: From Old French vire, from virer (“to turn”). Compare veer, vireton.

definition: Having the form of a straight rod; wand-shaped; straight and slender.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin virgāta, "yard" compared to "virga" as a measuring rod. Doublet of vergée.

definition: A certain function relating to a system of forces and their points of application.
etymology: From Latin vīs (vīs has a hidden "r" that shows in forms such as the genitive plural, vīrium).

definition: The quality or state of being virtual.
Having the power of seeing visions; inspired; also, seen in visions.
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: Destitute of vision; sightless.
Liable or subject to be visited or inspected.
A vista; a prospect.
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: Pertaining to, or involving, vitalism, or the theory of a special vital principle.
The act or process of vitalizing, or infusing the vital principle.
One of the oil tubes in the fruit of umbelliferous plants.
A genus of carnivores which comprises the civets.
An artificial division of vertebrates including those that produce their young alive.
The quality or condition of being viviparous.
A mask; a visor.
etymology: An alteration of visor by confusion of the ending.
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: The quality or state of being vocal; utterableness; resonance; as, the vocality of the letters.
The quality or state of being void.
etymology: From Middle English voidenesse, equivalent to void + -ness.

definition: (a) A flying fish of California (Exocoetus Californicus).
A cumbrous two-wheeled pleasure carriage used in Cuba.
The act or process of volatilizing, or rendering volatile; the state of being volatilized.
Discharged with a sudden burst, or as if in a volley; as, volleyed thunder.
In the greater part of Russia, a division for local government consisting of a group of mirs, or village communities; a canton.
etymology: Borrowed from Russian во́лость (vólostʹ) and Ukrainian во́лость (vólostʹ), from Old East Slavic волость (volostĭ).

definition: A tumbler; a leaper or vaulter.
etymology: Borrowed from French voltigeur, from voltiger (“to vault”), Italian volteggiare. See volt (“a tread”).

definition: The quality or state of being voluntary; spontaneousness; specifically, the quality or state of being free in the exercise of one's will.
Any theory which conceives will to be the dominant factor in experience or in the constitution of the world.
The principle of supporting a religious system and its institutions by voluntary association and effort, rather than by the aid or patronage of the state.
Any one of numerous species of large, handsome marine gastropods belonging to Voluta and allied genera.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin volūta (“a spiral scroll”). See volute.

definition: A genus of minute, pale-green, globular, organisms, about one fiftieth of an inch in diameter, found rolling through water, the motion being produced by minute colorless cilia.
etymology: From taxonomic name Volvox, from Latin volvō (“to roll”).

definition: (a) An abscess cavity in the lungs. (b) An abscess in any other parenchymatous organ.
etymology: Latin, from vomere (“to throw up, vomit”).

definition: Pertaining both to the vulva and the vagina.
To move staggeringly or unsteadily from one side to the other; to vacillate; to move the manner of a rotating disk when the axis of rotation is inclined to that of the disk.
etymology: Compare German wabbeln (“to wabble”), and English whap. Compare quaver.

definition: To attack or beat with a waddy.
A ravine through which a brook flows; the channel of a water course, which is dry except in the rainy season.
etymology: Ar. wadi a valley, a channel of a river, a river.

definition: A piece of plank two yard Bailey.
A horse imported from New South Wales; also, any Australian horse.
etymology: From (New South) Wale(s) + -er, the horse having been bred in the then colony of New South Wales in the 19th century.

definition: Any one of several species of kangaroos of the genus Macropus, especially M. robustus, sometimes called the great wallaroo.
etymology: Borrowed from Dharug walaru. Not, in fact, a blend of wallaby and kangaroo, although the fact that wallaroos are between wallabies and kangaroos in size may lead to that assumption.

definition: One who, or that which, wallows.
An exclamation of grief. [Obs. or Prov.
The common American eider.
Long and flexible, like a wand.
A boat for conveying provisions, tools, etc.
etymology: From Abenaki waniigan (“pit trap, container for sundries”); liken klahigan (“wooden trap”), Ojibwe waanikaan (“pit, excavated hole”).

definition: A pillow for the cheek; a pillow. [Obs. & R.] His bright helm was his wanger.
A surcingle, or strap of leather, used for binding a load upon the back of a beast; also, a leather tie; a short wagon rope.
etymology: From Middle English waynte, equivalent to womb + tie.

definition: Waning or diminished in some parts; not of uniform size throughout.
In some northern counties of England, a division, or district, answering to the hundred in other counties.
etymology: From Middle English wapentake, wepentake, wapentache, wapentac, from Old English wǣpenġetæc, from Old Norse vápnatak, from vápn (“weapon”) + taka (“take”), equivalent to weapon + take.

definition: (a) A fair-leader. (b) A rope with wall knots in it with which the shrouds are set taut.
etymology: From wap (“to wrap up”, dialectal). Compare warp

definition: The office of a ward or keeper; care and protection of a ward; guardianship; right of guardianship.
etymology: From ward + -ship. Cognate with Dutch waardschap, Central Franconian Wirtschaff, Hunsrik Wertschaft, German Wirtschaft.

definition: An American freshwater bream, or sunfish (Chænobryttus gulosus).
etymology: From war + mouth; the fish has stripes around the mouth that resemble war paint.

definition: The act of warping; also, a charge per ton made on shipping in some harbors.
Authorized by commission, precept, or right; justifiable; defensible; as, the seizure of a thief is always warrantable by law and justice; falsehood is never warrantable.
A bundle of straw, or other material, to relieve the pressure of burdens carried upon the head.
etymology: From Middle English wase (“torch”), related to Middle Low German and Middle Dutch wase (“bundle of straw, torch”), Danish vase (“wisp of straw, bundle”), Swedish vase (“a sheaf”).

definition: Pale or light blue.
etymology: From Middle English wachet, waget; compare French vaciet (“whortleberry”), Latin vaccīnium (“blueberry”).
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: A board set up to windward in a boat, to keep out water.
etymology: From Middle English water boarde, waterbord, equivalent to water + board.

definition: Furnished with wattles, or pendent fleshy processes at the chin or throat.
Free from waves; undisturbed; not agitated; as, the waveless sea.
The snow goose. [Canadian, & Local U. S.].
etymology: According to one theory, from Cree. An alternative etymology, perhaps a folk etymology, attributes the name to their peculiar, wavy flight.

definition: An exhibition of wax figures, or the place of exhibition.
A mark to guide in traveling.
A child or animal newly weaned; a wean.
Skillful in forecasting the changes of the weather.
Like a wedge; wedge-shaped.
Well. [Obs. or Scot.].
etymology: From Middle English wele, wyle, welle, likely a fusion of Old Norse vél ("device";

definition: (Zoöl.) (a) The common European sandpiper. (b) The chaffinch.
etymology: So called from its piping cry when disturbed.

definition: Any one of several species of edible marine fishes belonging to the genus Trachinus, of the family Trachinidæ. They have a broad spinose head, with the eyes looking upward.
etymology: From Middle English *wever, from Old Northern French wivre (“serpent”), from Latin vīpera. Doublet of wyvern and viper.

definition: Capable of being welded.
Prosperity; happiness; well-being; weal.
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: [OE. welken; cf.
etymology: From Middle English welken, probably from a continental Germanic language; compare Middle Dutch welken (Dutch welken) and Middle Low German welken. Cognate with German welken.

definition: Being well folded.
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: One who wishes well, or means kindly.
etymology: Possibly a calque of Latin benevolēns from bene (“well”) + volēns (“(one) wishing”).
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: Lit., world view; a conception of the course of events in, and of the purpose of, the world as a whole, forming a philosophical view or apprehension of the universe; the general idea embodied in a cosmology.
A Slavic tribe which once occupied the northern and eastern parts of Germany, of which a small remnant exists.
Passing to the west.
The distance, reckoned toward the west, between the two meridians passing through the extremities of a course, or portion of a ship's path; the departure of a course which lies to the west of north.
Dizzy; giddy.
etymology: From Middle English westi, westig (“desolate, deserted, lonely”), from Old English wēstiġ (“waste, deserted”), from wēste (“waste, desert”) + -iġ (“-y”). See waste.

definition: A form of vessel, often with steam power, having sharp ends and a very convex upper deck, much used on the Great Lakes, esp. for carrying grain.
etymology: * whale + back. * (ship): From its whale-like appearance when fully loaded.

definition: A man who owns, or has the care of, a wharf.
etymology: From Late Middle English wharfager (“keeper of a wharf”) (modified in the same way as messenger from Middle English messager, passenger from Middle English passager, etc.), from wharfage (“use of a wharf;

definition: One who rides a bicycle or tricycle; a cycler, or cyclist.
Circular; suitable to rotation.
A quantity; a goodly number. [Scot.].
etymology: From Middle English *wheen, quhein (also hwan, hwon, quhon), from Old English hwēne, hwǣne (“somewhat, a little”), instrumental form of hwōn (“little, few, a little, trifle, somewhat, a little while”).

definition: At what time soever; at whatever time; whenever.
etymology: From Middle English quen-so-ever, wensoever, whanne so evere, whan-so-ever, whan-so-evere, whenne-soever, when so evyr. By surface analysis, when + so + ever.

definition: At which; upon which; whereupon.
The act of one who, or that which, whiffs.
To waver, or shake, as if moved by gusts of wind; to shift, turn, or veer about.
etymology: 1662, in sense “flutter as blown by wind”, as whiff + -le (“(frequentative)”) and (onomatopoeia) sound of wind, particularly a leaf fluttering in unsteady wind; compare whiff.

definition: Formerly; once; of old; erewhile; at times. [Obs. or Poetic] Spenser.
etymology: From Middle English whilom (“(adverb) at one time, formerly, once; once upon a time; at times, sometimes; at a future time;

definition: Any one of several species of small curlews, especially the European species (Numenius phæopus), called also Jack curlew, half curlew, stone curlew, and tang whaup.
etymology: Uncertain. Perhaps from whimper + -el, alluding to the sound of its cry.

definition: A kind of hanger or sword used as a knife at meals and as a weapon. [Scot. & Prov.
A nematode worm (Trichocephalus dispar) often found parasitic in the human intestine.
A flock of snipe.
The skin of a newborn seal; also, the seal itself. [Sealers' Cant].
Like, or coming near to, white.
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: One who works in tinned or galvanized iron, or white iron; a tinsmith.
The spotted flycatcher.
To whatever place; to what place soever; wheresoever; as, I will go whithersoever you lead.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English whidersoevere. By surface analysis, whither + so + -ever.

definition: To make a rough, humming sound, like one who pronounces the letter r with too much force; to whir; to birr.
etymology: Probably of imitative origin. Cf. Hurr, Hurry, Whir.

definition: Somewhat wild; rather wild.
A spindle; a kind of reel; a winch.
A row or line of hay raked together for the purpose of being rolled into cocks or heaps.
A variety of winter apple of medium size, deep red color, and yellowish flesh of a rich, rather subacid flavor.
Having wings; rapid.
In a winning manner.
One who, or that which, winnows; specifically, a winnowing machine.
To kill by the cold, or exposure to the inclemency of winter; as, the wheat was winterkilled. [U. S.].
To show; to teach; to inform; to guide; to direct.
etymology: From Middle English wissen (“to instruct, enlighten, advise, admonish; guide, direct, control, manage, rule”), from Old English wisian (“to direct, instruct, guide, direct, rule; show, point out; declare, make known”).
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: Lit., wise men; specif. (A.-S. Hist.).
etymology: Learned borrowing from Old English witan, plural of wita (“wise man”).

definition: To reproach; to blame; to censure; also, to impute as blame. [Obs. or Scot.] Spenser.
etymology: From Middle English witen, from Old English wītan (“to see, accuse, go, depart”), from Proto-West Germanic *wītan, from Proto-Germanic *wītaną, from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see, find, behold”).

definition: Barium carbonate occurring in white or gray six-sided twin crystals, and also in columnar or granular masses.
etymology: After the English physician and mineralogist William Withering (1741-1799) in 1790.

definition: Tin ore freed from earthy matter by stamping.
A leguminous plant (Genista tinctoria) of Europe and Russian Asia, and adventitious in America.
An American shrub (Symphoricarpus occidentalis) which bears soft white berries.
Wonderfully; wondrously.
etymology: From Middle English wonderly, wonderli, wonderlich, from Old English wundorlīċ (“wonderful, miraculous”), from Proto-West Germanic *wundralīk, from Proto-Germanic *wundralīkaz, equivalent to wonder + -ly.
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: Struck with wonder, admiration, or surprise.
To dwell; to abide.
etymology: From Middle English wonen (“to abide, dwell”), from Old English wunian (“to dwell, be accustomed to”), from Proto-West Germanic *wunēn, from Proto-Germanic *wunāną (“to be wont;
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: The act or employment of cutting wood or timber.
Having a close texture; dense; as, a woofy cloud.
One who deals in wool.
A pack or bag of wool weighing two hundred and forty pounds.
etymology: From Middle English wolpak, wullepak, equivalent to wool + pack.

definition: A sack or bag of wool; specifically, the seat of the lord chancellor of England in the House of Lords, being a large, square sack of wool resembling a divan in form.
A species of steel imported from the East Indies, valued for making edge tools; Indian steel.
etymology: According to the American Heritage Dictionary, probably from a misreading of wook, an English transcription of (the root of) Kannada ಉಕ್ಕು (ukku),ಉರ್ಕು (urku, “steel”), Telugu ఉక్కు (ukku, “steel”);

definition: One of several pivoted pieces forming the throat of an adjustable die used in drawing wire, lead pipe, etc.
Without work; not laboring; as, many people were still workless.
One who, or that which, wounds.
Any one of certain plants whose soft, downy leaves have been used for dressing wounds, as the kidney vetch, and several species of the labiate genus Stachys.
A covering for the wrist.
One who wrongs or injures another.
Having the sails set in the manner called wing-and-wing. [Sailors' slang].
A species of elm (Ulmus montana) found in Northern and Western Europe; Scotch elm.
etymology: OE. wiche a kind of elm, AS. wice a kind of tree. Cf. Wicker.

definition: A narrow lane or alley. [Scot.] Jamieson.
etymology: From Middle English wynde, probably from wynden (“to wind, proceed, go”). Compare also Old English ġewind; Old Norse venda.

definition: A small three-masted vessel, with projecting bow stern and convex decks, used in the Mediterranean for transporting merchandise, etc.
etymology: From French chebec, from Spanish xabeque or Catalan xabec or Italian sciabecco, from Arabic شُبَّاك (šubbāk, “fishing-net”). Not to confuse with the sambuq, an Indian-Sea vessel.

definition: A genus of fishes comprising the common swordfish.
etymology: Borrowed from translingual Xiphias or Latin xiphiās (“swordfish”).

definition: (a) Like a sword; ensiform. (b) Of or pertaining to the xiphoid process; xiphoidian.
A gummy substance of the pentosan class, present in woody tissue, and yielding xylose on hydrolysis; wood gum.
A large Asiatic antelope (Budorcas taxicolor) native of the higher parts of the Himalayas and other lofty mountains.
A kind of demigod attendant on Kuvera, the god of wealth.
In China, the official headquarters or residence of a mandarin, including court rooms, offices, gardens, prisons, etc.; the place where the business of any public department is transcated.
To growl or snarl as a dog.
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: A shrub (Ilex Cassine) of the Holly family, native from Virginia to Florida.
etymology: From a Catawba word, most likely yap, yop, yą (“tree”), with the second element being either a diminutive suffix or pą (“leaf”) (resulting in the compound yąpą);

definition: To bring forth young, as a goat or a sheep; to ean.
etymology: AS. eánian, or geeánian; perhaps akin to E. ewe, or perhaps to L. agnus, Gr. Ean.

definition: The California poison oak (Rhus diversiloba).
An animal that yelps, or makes a yelping noise.
etymology: From Middle English yelpere; equivalent to yelp + -er. The avocet is so called from its sharp, shrill cry.

definition: The last night; the night last past.
etymology: From Middle English yesternyght, yisternight, from Old English ġiestranniht (“yesternight”), equivalent to yester- + night.

definition: Furious; mad; angry; fierce.
etymology: From Middle English yond, from Old English ġeond.
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: To pour water on; to soak in, or mix with, water. [Obs. or Prov.
etymology: From Middle English yoten, yeten (“to pour”), from Old English ġēotan (“to pour”), from Proto-West Germanic *geutan, from Proto-Germanic *geutaną (“to pour”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd- (“to pour”).

definition: To yell; to yowl.
usageNote: Marked obsolete or rare in Webster's 1913.

definition: A young person; a youth; also, any animal in its early life.
etymology: From Middle English youngling, ȝongelyng, ȝungling, from Old English ġeongling (“a youth, youngling”), from Proto-West Germanic *jungiling, from Proto-Germanic *jungalingaz, *jungilingaz (“young man, youngling”).

definition: The oxide, Y2O3, or earth, of yttrium.
etymology: From Ytterby, a town in Sweden.

definition: A species of Magnolia (M. conspicua) with large white blossoms that open before the leaves.
etymology: From Chinese Mandarin 玉蘭／玉兰 (yùlán) (lit. "jade orchid").

definition: A Turkish chief who supports a mounted militia bearing the same name.

A landowner; also, a collector of land revenue; now, usually, a kind of feudatory recognized as an actual proprietor so long as he pays to the government a certain fixed revenue. [Written also zemindar.] [India].
etymology: Borrowed from Urdu زمیندار (zamīndār, “landlord”), from Persian زمیندار.

definition: ZANTE CURRANT Zan"te cur"rant.
A cured olive which has spoiled or is on the verge of decomposition; loosely, an olive defective because of bruises, wormholes, or the like.
A species of macaque (Macacus pileatus) native of India and Ceylon.
A public shed, or portico, for travelers, worshipers, etc. [Burmah].
An Austrian silver coin equal to ten kreutzers, or about five cents.
In Russia, an elective local district and provincial administrative assembly.
etymology: From Russian зе́мство (zémstvo), from земля́ (zemljá, “land, country”).

definition: The part of a dwelling appropriated to women. [India].
etymology: From Hindi ज़नाना (zanānā), Urdu زنانه (zanānah), from Classical Persian زنانه (zanāna, “womanly”), from زن (zan, “woman”). Related to Old English cwene (“woman”). More at quean.

definition: A district or local division, as of a province. [India].
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi ज़िला (zilā) and Urdu ضلع (zilā), from Classical Persian ضلع (zil', “side, edge”), from Arabic ضِلْع (ḍilʕ, “side, edge, division”). Cognate with Nepali जिल्ला (jillā) and Marathi जिल्हा (jilhā).

definition: A salt of zirconic acid.
A grayish or whitish mineral occurring in orthorhombic, prismatic crystals, also in columnar masses.
etymology: Named after Austrian scientist Baron Sigmund Zois von Edelstein (1747-1819) in 1805. + -ite

definition: A European fresh-water bream (Abramis ballerus).
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from dialectal German Zope (French sope), probably from Slavic (compare Russian сапа́ (sapá)).

definition: Either one of two species of small African carnivores of the genus Ictonyx allied to the weasels and skunks. [Written also zoril, and zorille.].
etymology: Sp. zorilla, zorillo, dim. of zorra, zorro, a fox: cf. F. zorille.

definition: An exclamation formerly used as an oath, and an expression of anger or wonder.
etymology: Minced form of God's wounds, with reference to the wounds from Christ's crucifixion. Compare strewth, blimey, gadzooks, 'sblood, crikey.

definition: Am Austrian silver coin equivalent to 20 kreutzers, or about 10 cents.
The morbific principle of a zymotic disease.
